column1: What is the exact standard stud pitch (center-to-center spacing) in the Lego System grid, and in which axes does it apply?
column2: 8 mm, applied uniformly in both the X and Y horizontal axes.

column1: What is the height of a standard System brick, and how is it measured?
column2: 9.6 mm, measured from the bottom of the brick's wall to the top of its stud.

column1: What is the plate-to-brick height ratio, and why is this invariant critical?
column2: 3:1 — three stacked plates (3.2 mm each) always equal exactly one brick (9.6 mm) in height, enabling vertical alignment between plate-based and brick-based columns.

column1: Why does the stud itself add no height to a stacked column of bricks/plates?
column2: Because the stud inserts into the tube or anti-stud cavity of the element above, disappearing into the coupling geometry rather than contributing to stack height.

column1: What mechanical phenomenon produces 'clutch power' in a Lego stud-tube connection?
column2: Elastic interference fit: the tapered 4.8mm stud presses into the tube cavity, deforming the tube walls outward by a few hundredths of a millimeter; ABS's elastic recovery generates radial clamping force.

column1: What is the approximate friction coefficient between two clean ABS surfaces in a Lego joint?
Compare the approximate pull-apart (tensile) strength versus shear strength of a single new stud-tube joint.
column2: Tensile (pull-apart): ~2–3 newtons. Shear (sliding): ~5–10 newtons — shear is substantially stronger because the tube wall engages the stud along its full 1.7mm height, creating broader contact area and mechanical interlock.

column1: What is the key structural design implication of the shear-vs-tensile strength asymmetry in Lego joints?
column2: Builders must arrange elements so anticipated loads (wind, bumping, lateral pressure) act through the strong shear axis rather than the weak tensile/peel axis (lifting, bending, cantilever tipping).

column1: Where do Lego structural failures actually occur — within the ABS plastic or at the joints?
column2: At the interfaces between elements (studs peeling, tubes slipping, shear planes delaminating) — never within the ABS material itself, which can withstand extraordinary compressive loads (400+ kg for a single 2×2 brick).

column1: What is the first structural invariant of System building regarding overlap, and what happens if it's violated?
column2: A brick must engage at least two studs on the element beneath it to form a structural joint rather than a pivot; a single-stud connection allows rotation/tipping around that one point.

column1: What are the nominal stud outer diameter and anti-stud inner diameter values, and what interference do they create?
column2: Stud outer diameter: 4.80 mm; anti-stud inner diameter: 4.90 mm — creating a nominal 0.05 mm per-side diametric interference that produces clutch power.

column1: What dimensions does a standard 2×4 brick occupy in the horizontal plane, and from what invariant is this derived?
column2: 16 mm × 32 mm, derived directly from the 8 mm stud pitch invariant (2 studs × 8mm = 16mm; 4 studs × 8mm = 32mm).
